Type theory is well known to programmers (see TypeScript as an example, or the
currently very popular [TypeSafe.ai](https://docs.typesafe.ai/)).
In fact, due to programming, I grew up with type theory as a basis for my 
understanding of mathematics (and by extension programming), in contrast to 
most children, who are first introduced to set theory in school.

It does however intuitively make sense that these two theories are deeply
related: For example, we may have the set $\{0, 1\}$ and $\mathbb{N}$, both of
which _share_ one common element $0$, i.e. $0 \in \{0, 1\}$ _and_ $0 \in \mathbb{N}$.
In contrast to that, we may have the type $\texttt{Bool}$ with the _terms_
$0 : \texttt{Bool}$ and $1 : \texttt{Bool}$, and the type $\texttt{Nat}$ with
the _terms_ $0 : \texttt{Nat}$, $1 : \texttt{Nat}$, $2 : \texttt{Nat}$, etc. In
this case, we have _two different terms_ $0 : \texttt{Bool}$ and $0 :
\texttt{Nat}$, which are _not equal_ to each other.

There is however a connection which goes very deep, to places most
mathematicians do not dare to even go (and by extension most programmers will 
almost certainly never even hear about).
We use _Topos theory_ and its Mitchell–Bénabou language to connect set theory
with type theory.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
A _topos_ is a certain kind of category (see [this previous post](todo-add-correct-link)).
Concretely, a category $\mathcal{E}$ is an (elementary) topos if

1. it has all finite limits; in particular a _terminal object_ $1$, i.e. an
   object such that every $X$ admits a unique morphism $! : X \to 1$, and
   _pullbacks_;
2. it is _cartesian closed_, i.e. for all objects $X, Y$ there is an
   _exponential object_ $Y^X$ together with a natural bijection
   $$\text{Hom}_\mathcal{E}(Z \times X, Y) \cong \text{Hom}_\mathcal{E}(Z, Y^X);$$
3. it has a _subobject classifier_, i.e. an object $\Omega$ together with a
   morphism $\top : 1 \to \Omega$ such that for every monomorphism
   $m : A \rightarrowtail X$ there is a unique _characteristic morphism_
   $\chi_A : X \to \Omega$ making
   $$
   \begin{CD}
   A @>m>> X \\
   @V!VV @VV\chi_AV \\
   1 @>>\top> \Omega
   \end{CD}
   $$
   a pullback square.

See also [Definition 2.2 in my bachelor thesis](https://happel.ai/bachelor2).

:::

In particular, all presheaf categories are topoi, and the category of sets is a
topos, as it is the presheaf category of the terminal category 
(which has one object and one morphism).

As we now know that $\text{Set}$ is a topos, we can use the Mitchell–Bénabou language to reason about
it.
<!-- By this wangSketchesElephantIntroduction source, ... -->
By [@wangSketchesElephantIntroduction, Definition 2.2.2], we have that given a first order theory
$\mathcal{T}$, we associate to each type $T$ of it, an object $\llbracket T
\rrbracket$ in the model $\mathcal{C}$, a category which is a topos.
In particular, we associate to types $T$ the sets $\llbracket T \rrbracket$
under the assumption that $\mathcal{C} = \text{Set}$.
Similarly, we associate functions to function symbols and subobjects to relation
symbols.

For more information, [@wangSketchesElephantIntroduction] is a great book about
these ideas. Specifically, a _first-order theory_ $\mathbb{T}$ consists of
1. A collection of _types_ $A, B, C, \dots$
2. A collection of _function symbols_ $f, g, h, \dots$ each of which has a
  domain and codomain, i.e. $f : X_1 \times \dots \times X_n \to Y$
3. A collection of _relation symbols_ $R, S, \dots$ of the form
  $R \hookrightarrow X_1 \times \dots \times X_n$.

Then we can assign a _model_ to that theory, by having a category $\mathcal{C}$
and interpretation for each _type_, _function symbol_ and _relation symbol_:
1. $\llbracket A \rrbracket \in \text{Obj}(\mathcal{C})$
2. $\llbracket f \rrbracket \in \text{Hom}_\mathcal{C}(\llbracket X_1 \rrbracket\times\dots \llbracket X_n \rrbracket, \llbracket Y \rrbracket)$
3. $\llbracket R \rrbracket \in \text{Mono}_\mathcal{C}(\llbracket R \rrbracket ,\llbracket X_1 \rrbracket\times\dots \llbracket X_n \rrbracket)$

Now, given a typed first-order theory, we can therefore assign to each type $T$
a set, if we can model it in the category of sets $\text{Set}$. In TypeScript,
all types simply hold a set of possible values anyway, so it becomes
straightforward to make this formal, using the precise language of categorical
logic: As we have seen, given a type $T$, we can assign to it a set $\llbracket
T \rrbracket$ of possible values which inhabit that type.
